amendments.rule: **A purpose `לְ` + infinitive construct recast as a finite clause gives the complementizer to the preposition and the supplied subject and modal to the infinitive.** The ASV writes *that men may bring*, *that I may be glorified*. This is rule 48's division outside the privative `מִן`, and for the same reason: the complementizer is what the preposition contributes, while a supplied subject pronoun and a separately written modal belong to the verb, as rule 17 keeps a subject pronoun with its verb. The corpus puts the *that* on the preposition in 28 units across 17 chapters and never on the infinitive, so this too is settled. Where the ASV writes no English word at all for the preposition there is nothing to place, and the `לְ` goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **Read that as no word, not as no complementizer.** The complementizer is what a finite recasting spends on the preposition, but a recasting that makes the infinitive an English gerund or a bare verbal noun writes an ordinary preposition in that same position, and that word is the `לְ`'s on the same terms: `לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ` → *by keeping his covenant*, `לִשְׁלֹחַ מַלְאָכָיו` → *in sending his ambassadors*, `לְהָפֵר בְּרִית` → *by breaking the covenant*, `לָצֶקֶת` → *for casting*, `לֶאֱכֹל` → *an end of eating*. The corpus aligns a `לְ` before an infinitive construct to a written *to* in 583 units, to *that* in 81, and to *for*, *in*, *of*, *by*, *after* or *when* in 53 more, against 527 marked `unrepresented`; the two groups do not disagree, because every unrepresented one is a recasting that writes no function word at all — *left off building*, *the building of the house*. So ask whether a word is written before reaching for rule 40, and do not read the gerund itself as the recasting that silences the preposition. **Where two such `לְ` + infinitive phrases stand in one clause and the ASV writes one complementizer and one preposition, count them as this rule's last sentence directs rather than taking them in linear order.** `לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ לְעָמְדָהּ` → *that by keeping his covenant it might stand* gives *by* to the `לְ` of the gerund and *that* to the `לְ` whose infinitive the finite clause renders: the ASV fronts the complementizer ahead of the gerund adjunct, and that reordering says nothing about which preposition it answers to. **A temporal preposition before an infinitive construct is read the same way.** Where `בְּ` or `כְּ` + infinitive is recast as a finite temporal clause — `בְּחֻמָּם` → *When they are heated*, `בְּלֶכְתּוֹ` → *when he went*, `כְּבֹאֲךָ` → *When thou comest*, `כְּכַלֹּתְךָ` → *when thou hast made an end* — the preposition takes the *when*, the infinitive keeps the verb, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18. The corpus aligns `בְּ` to *when* in 45 units, so the temporal case is settled on the same footing as the purpose case. Read the preposition that is present rather than its lemma: a `לְ` heading such a phrase goes the same way even where its object is the noun rather than the infinitive, as in `לְקוֹל תִּתּוֹ` → *When he uttereth his voice*. **But only a preposition that still has an English word to take can take it.** Where no preposition is present and the construct relation itself is what the English *when* realizes, rule 19 puts that word on the *nomen rectum*, which is the infinitive: `עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ` → *at the time when it is trodden* gives *at the time* to `עֵת` and *when ... is trodden* to the infinitive. **And a preposition on which the ASV has already spent its own English word is in the same position as an absent one.** Where the preposition heads a construct noun, the ASV writes a word for that preposition and a second temporal word besides, the second answers to the construct relation and not to the preposition, so rule 19 puts it on the *nomen rectum*: `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` → *in the day when they shall make it* gives *in* to the `בְּ` and *the day* to `יוֹם`, leaving *when they shall make* to the infinitive, whose own suffix takes the pronoun rule 18 gives it. Count the ASV's function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s and rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s: a preposition holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, and giving it both would leave the construct's relation unrendered against rule 2. **Where no preposition stands before the infinitive construct at all, the English infinitive marker *to* belongs to the infinitive's own unit and is never `added`.** English writes no bare infinitive complement, so that word is what the infinitive itself licenses, exactly as rule 15 gives a supplied *a* to the noun that licenses it and rule 46 gives a supplied *them that* to a bare participle: `מֵאֵן בִּלְעָם הֲלֹךְ עִמָּנוּ` → *Balaam refuseth* ***to come*** *with us* and `הֲיָכוֹל אוּכַל דַּבֵּר מְאוּמָה` → *have I now any power at all* ***to speak*** *anything* each give the *to* to the infinitive, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24. Read whether a preposition is present before reaching for this sentence, since one and the same infinitive is read both ways in one chapter: `לַהֲלֹךְ עִמָּכֶם` → *to go with you* gives the written *to* to the `לְ` and only *go* to `הֲלֹךְ`, while the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds both words. And this reaches only a *to* the ASV has written: a modal's bare complement — *cannot go beyond* — has none to place, and a preposition the recasting leaves unrendered is `unrepresented` under rule 40 as before. **And the verb that takes such a bare *to* need not be an infinitive in the Hebrew.** Where a second Hebrew verb of any form — an imperative, a perfect, an imperfect — stands with no preposition on it and the ASV subordinates it to a governing verb as an English infinitive complement, the written *to* is what that English infinitive licenses and it joins the subordinated verb's own unit, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24, exactly as the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds it: `מַהֵר עֲנֵנִי` → *Make haste* ***to answer*** *me* gives *to answer* to `עָנָה` and *Make haste* to `מַהֵר`, and `אֵלֶיךָ כִסִּתִי` → *I flee unto thee* ***to hide*** *me* gives *to hide me* to `כָּסָה`. Read what the ASV made of the verb rather than what MACULA tags it, exactly as rule 19 reads a participle or infinitive the ASV has written as an English verb and rule 33 defers only to a governing verb the ASV has itself rendered as one. Do not give such a *to* to the governing verb: a verb already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and rule 44's supplied-preposition clause places a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object, which a complementizing *to* standing before a second verb is not. Two limits. Where a preposition morpheme does stand before that verb it takes the word first, on the terms above, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And where the governing verb and the subordinated verb are one and the same morpheme — a causative or other verb the ASV renders by a light verb and a second verb, as `הַשְׁמִיעֵנִי` → *Cause me* ***to hear*** and `הוֹשִׁיבַנִי` → *hath made me* ***to dwell*** — rule 44 keeps the whole phrase in that morpheme's one unit, headed on the lexical complement, and there is nothing to allocate.
amendments.why: Rule 52's closing sentence already gives a bare written *to* to a preposition-less infinitive construct, but says *infinitive construct*, so it does not reach a Hebrew verb of another form that the ASV subordinates as an English infinitive. PSA.143 writes that shape twice — `מַהֵר עֲנֵנִי` → *Make haste to answer me* (v. 7) and `אֵלֶיךָ כִסִּתִי` → *I flee unto thee to hide me* (v. 9), both imperative or perfect with no `לְ` on them — and a later pass reading the rule as printed would find no home for the word and mark it `added` under rule 30 or fold it into the governing verb. The extension is the rule's own reasoning (English writes no bare infinitive complement, so the word is licensed by the verb it stands on) read for what the ASV made of the verb rather than for what MACULA tags it, which is the same move rules 19 and 33 already make for a participle or infinitive written as an English verb. Both limits are stated so the widening cannot swallow settled cases: a present preposition keeps its priority, and the light-verb causative of v. 8 (`הַשְׁמִיעֵנִי` → *Cause me to hear*) stays one unit under rule 44 as this chapter and the corpus's light-verb units already read it. Nothing in the corpus tables contradicts it; the `לְ` counts cited in the rule are untouched, since every one of them has a preposition present.

conventions: An English lexical verb no morpheme's rendering completes is marked `added` in this chapter rather than folded into a preposition, a noun or the one Hebrew verb standing beside it: v. 6 *thirsteth*, supplied for the verbless colon `נַפְשִׁי כְאֶרֶץ עֲיֵפָה לְךָ` whose `לְ` keeps the *after* written for its own relation, and v. 9 *flee*, written beside the ASV's own *I ... to hide me* for the single verb `כִסִּתִי`. Rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause governs the first case in its own terms; the second is not literally a clause whose Hebrew has none, and the subtraction test is what decides it — dropping *flee* leaves `כָּסָה` its whole rendering in *hide*, so no written morpheme is diminished. The competing reading, taking *I flee ... to hide me* as one paraphrastic rendering of the one verb, is named in that unit's note.

report: Cross-verse: no split found. Every one of the 13 candidate lemmas differs because the ASV wrote different English for a difference the source licenses — possessive vs. object suffix throughout `הוּא`; `אוֹיֵב` absolute with a supplied *the* in v. 3 vs. construct `אֹיְבַי` in vv. 9 and 12; `לְפָנֶיךָ` split under rule 30's two-word test in v. 2 vs. bare `פָּנֶיךָ` in v. 7; `שְׁמַע` vs. hiphil `הַשְׁמִיעֵנִי`; `בְּ` rendered *on* before `פֹּעַל`/`מַעֲשֶׂה` in v. 5 and *in* before `חֶסֶד` in v. 12.

Read the dump end to end for what the lemma table cannot see, since it is keyed by source lemma and blind to `added` units. Supplied determiners go to the noun or construct that licenses them in all eight places (vv. 1, 3, 5 twice, 6, 7, 8, 10) under rules 15 and 29; supplied lexical verbs are marked `added` in both places they occur (v. 6 *thirsteth*, v. 9 *flee*); phrasal particles stay with the verb in all six (vv. 3, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12); substantival participles take their supplied *them that*/*those that* into their own unit in vv. 3, 7 and 12; the copula goes to the predicate while an explicit subject pronoun keeps only its own word in vv. 10 and 12 alike. No patch.

BSB: the single disagreement, the paragogic `ה` of `הַאֲזִינָה` in v. 1, is the convention difference rule 32 names by title — BSB attaches such a he to its host word. Not a genuine error; the ASV side is right to mark it `unrepresented`, and the token's *ear* gloss is the rule 39 reverse-distribution defect, as the verse note already says.

One edge a later reader may revisit, left as accepted and not patched: v. 11 `תוֹצִיא מִצָּרָה` → *bring my soul out of trouble* keeps *out* with the verb under rule 44's clause-level particle test and leaves `מִן` the bare *of*; the corpus's 838 `מִן` → *out of* units headed on *out* are the competing reading. Both are defensible and the accepted edge is contract-supported. The unit note does not name the alternative, which is a note deficiency rather than a wrong edge.

Amended rule 52 so that the bare English infinitive marker it already gives a preposition-less infinitive construct also covers a verb of any form the ASV subordinates as an English infinitive complement (vv. 7 *to answer*, 9 *to hide*), with both limits carved out: a present preposition takes the word first, and a causative rendered by a light verb plus a second verb (v. 8 *Cause me to hear*) is one unit under rule 44 with nothing to allocate. One convention recorded for the two `added` supplied lexical verbs; the chapter's other 18 repeated notes restate contract rules and are not logged.
